newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: BAAN FASTEST R&D GROWER IN NETHERLANDS.
newsitem.headline: BAAN FASTEST R&D GROWER IN NETHERLANDS.

text.p: Dutch software firm Baan Co's spending on research and development (R&D) grew by an average of 65 percent in the period 1990-1995, a survey by the Dutch Central Planning Bureau (CPB) showed on Wednesday.

The government advisory agency said this made Baan "R&D growth champion" among Dutch firms. Runners up are industrial moulds maker Axxicon, BE Semiconductor Industries (BESI), ASM Lithography, cable group Draka and unlisted gas turbines maker Thomassen Int.
On average, R&D spends of all Dutch firms rose by 3.5 percent per year between 1990 and 1995, the CPB said.
But it added that a number of "R&D intensive" companies had shown declining R&D spending during this period.
These included big internationals such as Philips Electronics, chemicals group DSM and biotechnology firm Gist-Brocades.
In terms of total R&D spends, the list was led by Philips, Shell, Akzo Nobel, Unilever and DSM.
Their R&D investments inside the Netherlands varied from 310 million guilders to 1.4 billion in 1995.
R&D spending of all companies in the Netherlands totalled 6.9 billion guilders in 1995, the report said.
The CPB said this figure included investments by many large international companies, which had chosen the Netherlands as the base for their European operations.

In the case of oil and chemicals groups this was due to the Netherlands' favourable geographic location. European centres for distribution of computers and electronics were attracted by Dutch logistic systems expertise and relatively favourable corporate taxes.
The bureau said it had noticed a trend whereby spending on radically innovative research was shifting to developing improvements of existing products.
The CPB warned this trend might hurt economic growth in the longer term. The more innovative products are, the more they contribute to growth, it added.

"The trend shift towards development may result in increasing numbers of products, but these will be very similar to existing ones and therefore offer a relatively limited boost to growth," the Central Planning Bureau said.
